items.prompt: The same true update — 'we raised $340 of $500, rain cut our selling time in half' — reads as reassuring to one person and alarming to another. What does that tell you?
choices: One version must contain different facts than the other
The facts and the effect of a message are two separate things — identical facts can land completely differently depending on who reads them
The alarmed reader simply misunderstood the message
This can only happen if the message was written carelessly
items.explanation: A message's facts and its effect are not the same axis. The same true statement can reassure one reader and alarm another, because the reader brings their own stakes and context to it — that gap is exactly what audience awareness manages.
items.reference:
Facts

What's true

Effect

Why: the same true statement can build trust with one reader and alarm another — truth and effect are separate axes.

Facts vs. effect

A message carries two separate things at once. They don't move together.

FactsEffect
NatureFixed, checkableDepends on the reader

The reader supplies half the equation — their own stakes and prior context decide how a fixed set of facts lands.

Common mistake

Treating a bad reaction as proof something false was said, or a good reaction as proof the message was complete. Neither follows — accuracy and effect are graded separately.

items.prompt: Someone says 'if a message lands badly, the writer must have said something untrue.' What's wrong with that claim?
choices: Nothing — a bad reaction always means an inaccurate statement
A message can be entirely accurate and still land badly, because 'landing badly' is about effect, not about truth — the facts and the effect are separate axes
It's only wrong for grown-up audiences
It's only wrong when the reader is older than the writer
items.explanation: A perfectly true message can still fail — burying the point, using the wrong tone, or leaving out the one thing the reader needed. Truth is necessary but not sufficient; audience awareness governs the effect, which truth alone doesn't guarantee.

items.prompt: Your teacher hears '$340 of $500' and immediately thinks about whether the trip is still affordable, not about what the rain did to foot traffic. Which lens is driving that reaction?
choices: Context
Incentives — what they personally care about based on how they interpret the message
Channel expectations
None of these — that reaction is unrelated to audience awareness
items.explanation: Incentives are about what the reader is personally on the hook for. Your teacher's incentive is the $500 goal, so that's the lens their attention runs through first, regardless of how interesting the rain story is.
items.reference:
🧠 Context — what do they already know?
🎯 Incentives — what do they personally care about?
📡 Channel — what does the medium train them to expect?

Why: every reader filters a message through all three lenses at once, whether the writer accounts for it or not.

items.prompt: You're telling the principal about the shortfall. Which of these is true audience awareness, and which crosses into something else?
choices: Telling the principal the trip is 'fully funded already' when it isn't yet
Leaving out exactly how the tables got rearranged in the rain, because it doesn't change what the principal needs to decide
Telling your groupmate a rosier number than your teacher, so they don't worry
Both A and C — adjusting the facts, not just the framing, for different audiences
items.explanation: Audience awareness changes what's foregrounded and how much detail is load-bearing — it never changes the underlying facts. Options A and C both alter the actual claim (funding status, the number) between audiences, which is deception, not calibration, and it gets caught the moment two audiences compare notes.
items.reference:
Changes

Foregrounding, detail, the ask

Never changes

The actual facts

Why: adjusting emphasis for a reader is calibration; adjusting the facts themselves is deception.
items.learnMore:
What's allowed to change

Changes (calibration)

  • Foregrounding
  • Level of detail
  • The ask

Never changes (or it's deception)

  • The actual facts
  • The real timeline
  • The real cause

Two versions of the same update can look very different in tone and length while agreeing on every checkable claim.

Common mistake

The moment two versions would contradict each other if compared side by side, it's no longer audience awareness — it's incompatible stories, and it gets caught the first time two readers compare notes.

items.prompt: A groupmate says 'just tell the principal it's basically handled' even though Saturday's make-up sale hasn't happened yet and could fall through. What's the audience-aware response?
choices: Say it's handled anyway — the principal doesn't need the caveats
Say a make-up sale is planned for Saturday, and flag if that plan is genuinely at risk
Give the principal the same detail you'd give your groupmate, so they can judge the risk themselves
Avoid mentioning it until Saturday actually happens
items.explanation: The principal doesn't need the operational detail, but they do need an accurate claim about status — 'planned for Saturday' is both scoped correctly and true. Saying 'basically handled' when it isn't is the facts-changing failure mode, not simplification; staying silent until Saturday denies them a decision-relevant fact (the shortfall) they may hear about elsewhere first.

items.prompt: You write an update quickly without thinking about who's reading it. What frame does it default to?
choices: A neutral, universally readable frame
The writer's own frame — usually the most detailed, least decision-oriented version possible
Whatever frame the last message in the thread used
The most simplified version, out of caution
items.explanation: There's no neutral default. Without a deliberate choice, a writer reverts to their own context and level of detail — typically over-detailed for a teacher and impenetrable for a principal who wasn't there. Audience awareness is the deliberate override of that default.
items.reference:
✍️ No deliberate choice
↓
📄 Defaults to the writer's own frame — most detailed, least decision-oriented

Why: there's no neutral default — without a deliberate choice, a writer reverts to their own context and vocabulary.

No deliberate choice about the reader
↓

↓

This isn't a rare failure — it's the default outcome of skipping straight to writing.

Common mistake

Trying to fix this by polishing prose after the fact. The fix is upstream: name the actual reader before writing the first sentence, not after the draft is 'done.'

items.prompt: Two kids send the same update about the bake sale shortfall. One thinks carefully about their reader first; the other just writes what's in their head. What's the most likely difference between the two messages?
choices: No real difference — a shortfall is a shortfall
The second message will tend to be more detailed and less decision-oriented, defaulting to the writer's own frame instead of the reader's
The second message will always be shorter
The second message will always be sent to the wrong person
items.explanation: Writing without deliberately considering the reader doesn't produce a random result — it reliably defaults toward the writer's own frame, because that's the frame already in their head. Audience awareness is an active correction against that default, not something that happens automatically.

items.prompt: Per L1, what are you supposed to figure out before writing anything that matters?
choices: What tone sounds the most polished
What the reader already knows and needs to act, what decision you want from them, and what they'd misread if you don't address it directly
How long the message should be, measured in words
Whether to use bullet points or prose
items.explanation: The three questions are about the reader's existing knowledge, the intended decision/reaction, and likely misreadings — all reader-facing, not stylistic. Format (length, bullets vs. prose) is a downstream choice, not the starting question.
items.reference:
① What do they know, and need to know to act?
② What decision/reaction am I trying to produce?
③ What will they misread if I don't address it?

Why: these three questions come before writing, not after — they decide what the message needs to contain.

The message just needs to be longer

items.prompt: Per L1, what's actually at stake when someone consistently fails to adjust their message for who's reading it?
choices: Nothing beyond mild reader annoyance
Credibility — someone who explains things the exact same way to a five-year-old and a room of adults comes across as not really understanding the room, however correct they are
Only the specific update being discussed, never their broader reputation
This only matters for people talking to school principals
items.explanation: The cost isn't just local clarity — it's a lasting read on the person's judgment. Someone who explains the exact same way regardless of who's listening is perceived as not reading the room, even when every fact they state is correct.
items.reference:
🧒 ↔ 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Same explanation, both audiences
⚠️ Reads as not reading the room

Why: adjusting register is itself read as a marker of seniority — failing to do it costs credibility even when every fact is correct.

Adjusting register isn't courtesy — readers use it as a proxy for whether someone understands the room.

Common mistake

Assuming 'staying consistent' is the safe, rigorous choice. It's actually read as not having modeled the audience at all.

items.prompt: Someone gives the exact same highly detailed explanation to everyone, from their groupmate to the principal. How is that likely to be perceived?

It has no effect on perception either way
Positively, since detail is always valued regardless of audience

Hitting the $500 goal in time for the trip — so the update should make clear whether that goal is still reachable
Getting every operational detail exactly right, same as a groupmate
Whether the trip happens at all, identical to the principal's incentive
items.explanation: The incentives lens ties directly to what the reader is accountable for. A teacher's stake is the $500 goal and the deadline, so a well-aimed update answers 'is this still reachable' early and explicitly, rather than leading with table logistics.

TeacherAccountable for the $500

items.prompt: Why does leading with the bottom line matter more for a message to the principal than a quick text to your groupmate?
choices: The principal is less capable and needs the conclusion spelled out
The medium is different, so grammar rules change
The principal has less time and context invested per message, so they need the outcome before deciding whether to keep reading
It doesn't actually matter more — leading with the point is equally important everywhere
items.explanation: Your groupmate already has shared context and is continuing a conversation, so leading with detail before the point is low-cost. A principal reading a one-line update with no shared context will start worrying before reaching a buried conclusion — putting the outcome first respects that their attention is the scarce resource, not their understanding.
items.reference:
💬 Groupmate text — informal, detail can come first
📢 Principal update — cold read, bottom line first

Why: BLUF matters more the less shared context and time the reader has invested — it's about their attention, not their intelligence.

items.prompt: The principal asks you a narrow, specific question about how many tables you had at the sale. Per L3's 'role vs. stake' failure mode, how should you calibrate your answer?
choices: Always give the short, big-picture version to anyone in charge

Redirect them to your teacher, since the principal shouldn't be asking operational questions

items.explanation: L3 is explicit: someone asking a narrow, specific question is signaling they want the detailed answer to that question, even if their role would normally get the short version. items.prompt: You send your teacher a message that says 'just so you know, the bake sale was slower than expected' with no further detail. What failure mode is this, per L3?
choices: Correct — teachers prefer brief, low-detail updates

This is fine as long as the facts are accurate

items.explanation: An ambiguous 'just so you know' forces the reader to guess whether a response, decision, or action is expected — that's a failure of audience awareness even if every stated fact is true, because it doesn't answer the teacher's real question ('is the goal still reachable, and do you need something from me').
